matchups.name: esper blink
matchups.stance_rationale: Their interaction is one-for-one - 4 Fatal Push and 3.6 Solitude across 10 of 10 lists in the 2026-09-10 capture - and their engine is recursion, so the only sideboard card that changes this matchup is one that refills faster than they trade. Nothing in our fifteen answers Overlord of the Balemurk and nothing needs to: the 60 curves under it and Ocelot Pride rebuilds through a one-for-one exchange for free.

In 10 of 10 pulled boards at 2.1; its static line stops activated abilities of creatures, which is Ranger-Captain of Eos's sacrifice ability and transformed Ajani's loyalty abilities
In 9 of 10 pulled boards at 2.2; caps a deck built on twelve one-drops at a single spell per turn
In 9 of 10 pulled boards at 2.1; strips a nonbasic from a manabase carrying only four basic lands

survives_opposing_board.why: Its chapter abilities are triggered rather than activated, so a resolved Clarion Conqueror does not switch them off, and chapter I banks three playable cards on the turn it lands - a later Wrath of the Skies at X=4 cannot take those back.

opponent_plan.posture_why: Recursion and flicker value bury a one-for-one exchange over eight turns rather than racing our clock with damage.

key_cards.why: The 4-of recursion engine that returns a creature or planeswalker out of their graveyard every time it is impended or cast
Exiles and returns their own Solitude for a second free removal trigger every combat step
Free removal for our best attacker on a turn we are tapped out, at the cost of a white card
The postboard reset that answers the token board Ocelot Pride and Ajani build

play_plan.keep: Two lands and two one-drops, or one land and Ocelot Pride plus Guide of Souls.
play_plan.goldfish_for: Turn-one Ocelot Pride, turn-two Guide of Souls plus a second one-drop, so the end-step trigger is live before Solitude.
play_plan.watch_for: Whether they hold two white sources for Solitude, and whether Phelia, Exuberant Shepherd is out to rebuy it.
play_plan.posture_why: Their engine wins any long game, so the clock has to be lethal before Overlord of the Balemurk stabilises.

notes: Ranger-Captain of Eos's sacrifice ability stops noncreature spells for the turn: hold it for the turn they untap with three mana and a Wrath of the Skies, not for a Fatal Push.

matchups.name: broodscale bloodchief
matchups.stance_rationale: This is the largest deck in the recorded field at 6.95pp and it kills out of nowhere off an artifact engine. Our maindeck has no answer to an artifact or to Urza's Saga, so all four of the in-cards attack the pieces rather than the creature: Wrath of the Skies destroys artifacts as well as creatures, Wear kills Blade of the Bloodchief, Obsidian Charmaw is discounted to {1}{R}{R} by their own colorless lands, and Orim's Chant buys the turn we need to finish.

In 8 of 10 pulled boards at 1.2; the only creature in their pool that outsizes a 4/4 Obsidian Charmaw

A one-mana instant; no pulled board carries a counterspell, and Trinisphere taxes it to three, which is still castable on the turn it matters.

Blade of the Bloodchief is a 3-of artifact in 10 of 10 recorded lists and Springleaf Drum is in all ten; Wear answers either at instant speed for two mana, and Nature's Claim can only trade with it one-for-one.

Our fifteen is nine hosers aimed at combo, graveyards, artifacts and greedy manabases, and not one of them beats a deck playing our own cards; the mirror is decided inside the 60 by Galvanic Discharge, the energy Guide of Souls banks, and who gets Ocelot Pride's end-step trigger online first.

sideboard_audit.why: Four of the recorded field's fifteen rows run a manabase it strands - eldrazi ramp's four Eldrazi Temple and four Ugin's Labyrinth, dimir control's fifteen nonbasics against one Swamp, dimir frog's Polluted Delta and Watery Grave shell, and 45c aggro's twelve fetchlands behind one Plains and one Mountain, where it also takes away the domain count Leyline Binding and Scion of Draco are priced off. It is the only card in the box that answers a mana advantage rather than a permanent, and the sideboard copy exists because the maindeck one is a card we do not want to draw in the other eleven rows.

The four rows it serves are the field's multi-spell decks: devoted combo needs a tutor and a combo piece in one turn, living end needs a cascade and the spell it casts, and both prowess rows need a second spell each turn for Cori-Steel Cutter. Two copies because it is the card those matchups have to answer and 9 of 10 recorded boros lists agree.

It is priced by the two rows it serves rather than by its printed cost: eldrazi ramp and broodscale bloodchief both run four Eldrazi Temple and colorless lands beside it, so the reduction makes it a turn-three {1}{R}{R} 4/4 flier that also destroys Urza's Saga or Ugin's Labyrinth. Three copies because both rows want to see it early, and it is a threat as well as an answer.

One copy of a one-mana instant against the two rows whose kill happens on a single identifiable turn. Broodscale bloodchief at 6.95pp is the largest deck in the recorded field and devoted combo at 4.77pp is the fourth; against both, buying the turn is worth as much as answering a permanent, and kicked it also stops a Craterhoof Behemoth attack.

One copy, because the three rows it serves are all one-card matchups - Goryo's Vengeance and Living End both read the graveyard and both become blanks - and because a second copy is dead in the other twelve. It is a white enchantment, so Consign to Memory, the most-boarded card in the recorded field, cannot answer it.

The two rows it serves are the field's attrition decks: esper blink trades one-for-one with Fatal Push and Solitude, and dimir control counters or removes each threat as it lands. It is the only card in our fifteen that generates cards rather than answering permanents, and it is an enchantment, which neither row's pulled boards can destroy.

It is not graveyard hate: it counters a spell cast with no mana spent, which is Violent Outburst's cascade, Force of Negation's alternate cost and evoked Solitude. All three rows it serves run at least two of those in 10 of 10 recorded lists, and against living end it is specifically the card that counters the Force of Vigor that would answer the rest of our hate.

Wear // Tear is two answers on one card and all four rows it serves have targets on both types: boros ponza runs 2.7 maindeck Relic of Progenitus and boards 3.7 High Noon, pinnacle affinity runs four Weapons Manufacturing and 3.6 Mox Opal, broodscale bloodchief runs three Blade of the Bloodchief, and 45c aggro runs four Leyline of the Guildpact and four Scion of Draco, which is an Artifact Creature. Fused for {1}{R}{W} it answers one of each.

Two copies because it is the only card in our fifteen that answers a board rather than a permanent, and because it is symmetric - the three rows it serves are the ones whose board is worth more than ours by turn three. Against pinnacle affinity it destroys artifacts too, which is the whole of their deck rather than half of it.

deck_tech.name: How much energy Galvanic Discharge spends
deck_tech.quirk: Galvanic Discharge gives three energy and then lets you pay any amount of it, so the choice is how much of the deck's other energy sink you spend killing this creature.

lines.why: One damage kills Monastery Swiftspear, Dragon's Rage Channeler and a turn-one Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer before they grow, and banks two energy for Guide of Souls.
Psychic Frog, Orcish Bowmasters, Phelia, Exuberant Shepherd and a mirror Guide of Souls all die to two, which still leaves one energy banked.
Against a combo deck the creature has to die now; banking energy for a flying attack is a plan that assumes a turn six these matchups do not give us.
Default to the least energy that kills the creature. The surplus is what pays for Guide of Souls's attack trigger, and that trigger is the deck's only evasion.

deck_tech.name: The Ocelot Pride end-step loop
deck_tech.quirk: The token engine is a loop, not a card: each new creature feeds Guide of Souls, which feeds Ocelot Pride's end-step check, which makes the next creature.
loop: A creature enters, so Guide of Souls triggers: gain one life and bank one energy.
At our end step Ocelot Pride sees that we gained life this turn and makes a 1/1 Cat.
With the city's blessing, Ocelot Pride then copies every token that entered this turn, so the board doubles rather than grows by one.
Ajani, Nacatl Pariah's 0 ability and Voice of Victory's mobilize add more bodies, each of which re-triggers Guide of Souls and restarts the loop next end step.

lines.mode: hold the tokens on the battlefield
lines.why: Against one-for-one removal the board is the resource; each Cat costs them a card and none of them can answer the end-step trigger itself.
Against a sweeper or a combo turn, sacrifice to Goblin Bombardment in response: ten tokens on the battlefield are worth nothing after a Wrath of the Skies and ten damage before it.

deck_tech.name: Blood Moon first or fetchlands first
deck_tech.quirk: Our own manabase is fourteen nonbasics and four basics, so a resolved Blood Moon turns ten fetchlands into Mountains with no activated ability at all - the sequencing decides whether it is a Time Walk for us or for them.

lines.mode: fetch a basic Plains, then cast Blood Moon
lines.why: White is the colour we cannot lose - eleven of our nonland cards need it - so the Plains has to be on the battlefield before the enchantment resolves.

lines.mode: leave Blood Moon in hand and keep the fetchlands live
lines.why: These rows play basics or a manabase close enough to ours that the tax lands on us, so our own fixing is worth more than their inconvenience.
If the maindeck copy is the only spell in hand and both basics are already down, cast it; otherwise it is a fetchland that draws no cards.

meta_calls.why: It counters a triggered ability for one blue mana, and this deck is triggered abilities. Above that bar the cards whose value is an enters trigger stop being reliable.
meta_calls.cost: Seasoned Pyromancer and The Legend of Roku are our two best cards against removal-heavy decks, and Lightning Bolt trades card advantage for damage that cannot be countered this way.

gaps.why: The mirror - under either of the field's two labels for it - is served by no card in our fifteen, and the boarding plan for it is zero swaps. Every sideboard slot is aimed at a graveyard, an artifact, a free spell or a nonbasic manabase; the only one with a live target is Tear on a maindeck Blood Moon or Goblin Bombardment, and both of those are cards we play ourselves, so the swap is card-neutral and tempo-negative in a race. The matchup is decided inside the maindeck, which means the sideboard is doing nothing in 2.29pp of the recorded field (3.68pp if the separate 'boros energy' row at 1.39pp is counted, which the aliases map in .protocol/raw-matchups.json says it should be).

This is the worst recorded matchup in the field at 0.4494 over 453 matches and the plan does not fix it, it only attacks it. Trinisphere is in 10 of 10 pulled boards at 2.6 copies and every card in our 60 costs one to three mana; we have no answer to a resolved copy at all, and Obsidian Charmaw and Blood Moon are both three-mana plays that a Trinisphere on turn three arrives ahead of on the play.
